title: How a decorator differs from a handler chain, and what wrapping does to identity

questions.stem: Slack(Sms(Email)) sends one alert. Compared with a Chain of Responsibility, which layers run?

options.text: The first layer able to handle it, since a layer that deals with the alert stops the call there.
options.says: That is how a Chain of Responsibility behaves: a handler may stop the request. The page says a decorator does not.

options.text: Every layer, since each one does its own work and then calls the notifier it wraps.
options.says: The page's Q3: a decorator always delegates to the next wrapper, so Email, SMS and Slack all execute.

options.text: The layer the client picks, since the client chooses one layer for each alert it sends.
options.says: Picking one algorithm from several describes Strategy, whose alternatives are not cumulative.

questions.stem: Notifier original is an EmailNotifier, and Notifier decorated is original wrapped in an SmsDecorator. What is original == decorated?

options.text: false, because decorated refers to a different object that holds original.
options.says: The page lists this pitfall: wrapping creates a new instance, so == between the wrapper and the wrapped object is false.

options.text: true, because decorated forwards every call to original and so is original.
options.says: Forwarding calls does not make two objects one; == compares references, and the decorator is its own instance.

options.text: true when EmailNotifier overrides equals, because == then compares the addresses.
options.says: == compares references and never calls equals, so overriding equals changes nothing here.

origin.section: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
